findings.claim: -5 F1 and -4.polisher are only partly resolved. The test still gives a false failure on 64 KiB-page Linux, which is the case those findings named. The new ARG_MAX guard (line 111) skips only the past case. The under case is always run, and it is just 128 identifiers (2,304 bytes) smaller. So whenever pastN*18 >= ARG_MAX/2, the under case also passes about half of ARG_MAX or more as sh arguments, and the guard's own comment (lines 109-110) says that size may fail the exec of sh. Concrete case: 64 KiB pages with an 8 MiB stack. getconf gives PAGESIZE 65536 and ARG_MAX 2097152, so bound = 2097152. The past case is skipped. The under case passes 116,444 arguments: about 2,096,000 string bytes plus about 930 KB of argv pointers, which the kernel counts against the same stack/4 limit of 2 MiB. Either the exec of sh fails with E2BIG, or the about 2 MB EVIDENCE_WANT plus the rest of the environment passes the 2 MiB total when sh execs awk. In both cases wantResult(0, 'no' lines) fails. The comment at lines 72-73 ('so the test holds on every page size') is therefore wrong on 64 KiB pages. The 16 KiB-page case works: bound 512 KiB, both cases are well under ARG_MAX, and awk fails only on MAX_ARG_STRLEN. A fix is to apply the same guard to the under case, or to skip the whole subtest, when the under bytes plus 8 bytes of pointer per argument reach the limit.

The ARG_MAX guard counts only the joined string bytes (pastN*18). The kernel also counts one pointer for each argument, 8 bytes on 64-bit, which adds about 44% for 18-byte identifiers. It also counts the test process's own environment. So 'half of ARG_MAX' is a heuristic, and the margin is not computed from what exec actually counts. No realistic host is shown to fall between the guard and the real limit. This is a precision gap in a new guard, not a reproduced failure.

The new helper's doc says 'no read is missed whatever its subscript or blanks', but the rule checks only what follows the read. A read with a prefix operator, such as `-ENVIRON["X"] ""`, `!ENVIRON["X"] ""` or `++ENVIRON["X"] ""`, matches the forced pattern and is accepted. In awk, unary minus and not bind tighter than concatenation, so the value is made a number before the "" is appended. The class the lint exists for, an environment value taken as a number, can therefore pass it. evidence.sh has no such read today. The T4q rule had the same gap, but the T4r helper now states that it finds every read. A row such as `x = -ENVIRON["X"] ""` in TestUnforcedEnvironReadsFindsEveryRead, and a refusal of a preceding unary operator, would close the gap.

The pin for -3 F1 checks only that the text `ids[i] = ids[i] ""` appears somewhere in evidence.sh. A comment containing that text, or the statement moved to after `wanted[ids[i]] = 1`, would keep the test green while the keys are again built from untouched split elements. L80 accepts a text pin, so -3 F1 is resolved as L80 says. Anchoring the needle to the whole statement `{ ids[i] = ids[i] ""; wanted[ids[i]] = 1 }` would hold the order too.

`underN = bound/joined - 64` is not checked for being positive. The page size is only checked to be 1 or more (line 89), so a getconf PAGESIZE under 36 bytes makes underN negative, and make([]string, underN) in manyIDs panics instead of failing with a message. No real Linux page size is that small, so realistic input does not reach this. It is the hunt row's negative-size class on a new computation.
